name: bddisasm
baseline: Capstone (decode+format throughput); Zydis and Intel XED also measured in the same harness
workload: Decoding (and decoding plus formatting) the code section of a 64-bit x86 binary repeatedly in the disas-bench harness, reported as MB/s of machine code.
claimed_speedup: disas-bench charts (approximate readings): on the Ryzen 9 9950X bddisasm decode+format is about 47 MB/s (mini decoder about 49) versus Capstone about 28 MB/s, and decode-only about 106 MB/s (mini about 180); on the i9-13900K decode+format about 36 (mini about 39) versus Capstone about 26, decode-only about 103 (mini about 180). Ratio to Capstone on decode+format about 1.7x (AMD) and 1.4x (Intel) (derived from page data, chart readings). README alone gives 'around 240 CPU clocks per decoded instruction (~12M decoded instructions per second)' for the legacy decoder and about 150 clocks for the mini decoder on an Intel Core Ultra 7 165H, with no baseline.
compiler_and_flags: Capstone and XED harnesses: cc main.c -O3 (GCC 13.3 on the AMD run, GCC 14.2 on the Intel run); Zydis and bddisasm via CMake Release (bddisasm with BDD_LTO=ON); XED built with mfile.py --opt=3 (bench/cs/Makefile, bench/xed/Makefile, make-all.sh)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X (Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 6.8.0) and Intel Core i9-13900K (Debian trixie, Linux 6.12.48)
tradeoffs: C library with Python and Rust bindings, directly usable from C++. Includes a 'mini' decoder with reduced detail and a shellcode-detection emulator (not benchmarked). Decode+format advantage over Capstone is modest.
caveats: Smaller win than iced, yaxpeax and diStorm; the README's own throughput numbers carry no baseline. Chart values are visual readings of bar-chart PNGs (approximate, roughly +/-3 MB/s), not a text table. Capstone appears only as a decode+format row, so decode+format rows are the like-for-like comparison; formatted output differs in detail between libraries. The input binary and the harness's disassembly mode details were not examined. Baseline Capstone was not benchmarked against libopcodes/objdump here.

name: diStorm3
baseline: Capstone, Zydis, Intel XED, bddisasm, udis86 and BeaEngine (other x86/x86-64 disassembler libraries)
workload: Decoding only, and decoding plus formatting, of the 77 MB code section of Firefox 86's 64-bit xul.dll, looped 20 times, measured in MB/s.
claimed_speedup: Decode plus format: 58.85 MB/s versus Zydis 22.24, bddisasm 16.00, XED 15.67, Capstone 14.02, BeaEngine 13.42, udis86 12.02 MB/s (about 4.2x Capstone, derived from page data); second only to iced (149.21). Decode only: 92.17 MB/s versus XED 55.39, Zydis (min) 61.33, bddisasm 35.48, Zydis 34.19, udis86 80.72 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: Linux (Kubuntu 21.04), gcc 10.3.0 and Rust 1.52.1. The C libraries are built by make-all.sh in the benchmark repo (CMake Release builds with CFLAGS=-flto, BeaEngine -O3 -flto); the Rust benchmark programs are built by their own per-library Makefiles, whose flags were not inspected.
tradeoffs: Plain C with a single API (about 45 KB per its README), callable directly from C++. Decodes x86/AMD64 only; coverage of recent instruction-set extensions was not checked.
caveats: The table is from the iced author's disas-bench fork (June 2021, i5-6600K) with the diStorm of that date; the last commit on the default branch is December 2021, so newer instruction sets are probably missing. The README itself only quotes a 2014 thesis ('chose diStorm3, which had the best performance') and gives no numbers. Decode and decode+format throughput, not assembler speed; baselines are not GNU as, NASM or MASM.

name: iced (iced-x86)
baseline: Capstone, Zydis and Intel XED (other x86/x86-64 disassembler libraries; objdump was not tested)
workload: Decoding only, and decoding plus formatting, of the 77 MB code section of Firefox 86's 64-bit xul.dll, looped 20 times, measured in MB/s of machine code.
claimed_speedup: Decode only: 256.69 MB/s versus XED 55.39, Zydis (min) 61.33, Zydis 34.19, bddisasm 35.48, diStorm 92.17 MB/s. Decode plus format: 149.21 MB/s versus diStorm 58.85, Zydis 22.24, XED 15.67, Capstone 14.02 MB/s (about 10.6x Capstone, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Linux (Kubuntu 21.04), gcc 10.3.0 and Rust 1.52.1. The C libraries are built by make-all.sh in the benchmark repo (CMake Release builds with CFLAGS=-flto, BeaEngine -O3 -flto); the Rust benchmark programs are built by their own per-library Makefiles, whose flags were not inspected.
tradeoffs: Rust crate (bindings for .NET, Java, Python, Lua, JavaScript via WebAssembly per its README); no C or C++ API in the repo, so C++ projects need FFI. Decoded instruction is 40 bytes and the decoder allocates nothing. Also contains an encoder and a code assembler.
caveats: The icedland/disas-bench repo is hosted by iced's own organisation (the original harness is athre0z's, per the MIT copyright line, 2017), so it is not a fully independent run; the published table is from June 2021 on a Skylake i5, with library versions of that date. The numbers are decode and decode+format throughput, not assembling speed, so GNU as, NASM and MASM are not the compared baselines. Capstone has no decode-only mode, so it appears only in the format table. Rust and C libraries use different formatters, so the decode+format column is not like for like in output text. A later fork by the yaxpeax author (i7-12700K, GCC 11, rustc 1.67 nightly, bar chart without numbers) shows iced decode at roughly 350 MB/s and yaxpeax-x86 about level with it (values read off the bars, so approximate).

name: Minotaur
baseline: LLVM -O3 (clang) output quality, i.e. LLVM's own peephole and vectorization passes
workload: Runtime of code compiled with and without the Minotaur LLVM pass: SPEC CPU 2017, the GMP benchmark suite and LibYUV.
claimed_speedup: OOPSLA 2024 paper, per WebSearch result text only (paper not opened): SPEC CPU 2017 mean speedup 1.5% on Intel (1.2% on AMD) with a maximum of 4.5% on 638.imagick; GMP benchmark suite mean 7.3% with a maximum of 13% on an Intel Cascade Lake processor; LibYUV geomean 1.029x on AMD Zen 3.
hardware: Intel Cascade Lake (GMP), AMD Zen 3 (LibYUV); other CPUs per paper not confirmed
tradeoffs: Runs as an LLVM opt pass or via minotaur-cc / minotaur-c++ wrappers; needs a patched, RTTI- and EH-enabled LLVM build, Alive2, Z3 and Redis (offline cache mode), which makes the build heavy. Synthesis time adds to compile time.
caveats: All numbers come from search-result text of the paper (arxiv 2306.00229, blocked in this environment) and have not been checked on the paper itself; the repo README has no performance numbers and no evaluation directory was seen. Gains on SPEC are small (1.2-1.5% mean). Peer review (OOPSLA 2024) taken from a SPLASH 2024 programme page snippet. It is an LLVM IR superoptimizer, so only loosely 'assembly tooling'.
found_via: WebSearch 'superoptimizer outperforms gcc -O3 ...' and 'Minotaur SIMD-oriented superoptimizer LLVM evaluation speedup SPEC CPU 2017 geomean results'; opened github.com/minotaur-toolkit/minotaur

name: STOKE
baseline: gcc -O3 and icc -O3 compiled x86-64 code (output quality); expert hand-written assembly for some kernels; Google Native Client's shipped libc string functions in the 2017 paper
workload: Runtime of superoptimized loop-free x86-64 kernels (OpenSSL big-number Montgomery multiplication, Hacker's Delight, SAXPY, linked-list traversal) starting from llvm -O0 code, and 13 libc string functions from NaCl newlib.
claimed_speedup: ASPLOS 2013 paper (PDF opened): the Montgomery multiplication kernel from OpenSSL's big-number library is 16 lines shorter and 1.6x faster than gcc -O3 output and slightly faster than expert handwritten assembly; across the benchmark kernels STOKE matches gcc -O3 and icc -O3 starting from llvm -O0 and in several cases exceeds both. ASPLOS 2017 paper (PDF opened): 'median and average speedup of 25% over the libraries shipped by Google' for 13 libc string functions with formal verification. README tutorial: popcount drops from about 1.05 s to about 0.13 s versus a g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -fno-inline build.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 and icc -O3 baselines (versions not stated in the extracted paper text); gcc-4.9 used in the 2017 paper's translation mode; README tutorial uses g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -fno-inline
hardware: ASPLOS 2013: synthesis and optimization on a cluster of 40 dual-core 1.8 GHz AMD Opterons (machine used for the runtime speedups not identified in the extracted text); ASPLOS 2017: machines with two Intel Xeon E5-2667v2 3.3 GHz processors and 256 GB RAM
tradeoffs: x86-64 only and Intel-microarchitecture oriented. Needs test cases plus bounded or SMT-based equivalence checking, search budgets of tens of minutes per kernel on a cluster, and works best on short loop-free sequences. README: 'STOKE isn't production ready' and 'nobody is actively working on this code base'; it says it is 'not quite at the point where we can take a generic loop and expect to improve gcc/llvm -O3 code'.
caveats: Speedups are on hand-picked small kernels, and the ASPLOS 2013 Figure 11 reports speedup over llvm -O0 with STOKE 'comparable' to gcc -O3 and icc -O3 on many kernels, not always faster. The 2017 baseline is Google's shipped NaCl libc code (already constrained by SFI alignment rules), not a plain gcc -O3 build. A 2022 TU Delft bachelor thesis, seen only as a WebSearch snippet (not opened), reports that STOKE often fails to match gcc -O3 and struggles with loops. Not a benchmark of assemble time. Same repo holds both papers (docs/papers/asplos13.pdf, asplos17.pdf, cacm16.pdf and others).

name: Unison
baseline: LLVM's register allocator and instruction scheduler (output quality, Hexagon, ARM and MIPS back ends)
workload: Estimated speedup and code size of functions from MediaBench and SPEC CPU2006 compiled with Unison's integrated combinatorial register allocation and instruction scheduling versus LLVM.
claimed_speedup: Per WebSearch result text of the arXiv/TOPLAS paper only (paper not opened): mean estimated speedup ranges from 1.1% to 10% and mean code size reduction from 1.3% to 3.8% depending on the architecture; the authors say execution on Hexagon confirms that the estimated speedup becomes actual speedup.
hardware: Hexagon (execution check); estimates for ARM and MIPS
tradeoffs: Haskell tool driving constraint solvers, used through a Unison-enabled LLVM fork (github.com/unison-code/llvm); solving time is far higher than LLVM's heuristics; targets Hexagon, ARM and MIPS rather than x86.
caveats: Numbers are 'estimated' speedups from a static cost model, not measured runtimes, except for the Hexagon confirmation. The repo README has no performance claims or links to results, and the paper and project site were not reachable here, so all numbers are from search-result text. Peer review (ACM TOPLAS 2019 journal version) inferred from a doi 10.1145/3332373 snippet. Last commit is 2023.

name: aron
baseline: macOS as (the system assembler on macOS, not GNU as)
workload: Assembling the repo's test.macos.s file (x86-64) with aron versus the macOS assembler.
claimed_speedup: 'aron is 12.94 ± 2.34 times faster than as' (text of the README benchmark image).
tradeoffs: Incomplete x86-64 assembler (README says so); outputs ELF and Mach-O objects; supports only part of the instruction set and directives, so it cannot replace GNU as, NASM or MASM on general input.
caveats: The README says 'This is not empirical by any means'. One input file, no command, hardware or flags stated, and the baseline is macOS as rather than GNU as. The language is inferred from Cargo.toml and rustfmt.toml because the repo page shows no language bar. The speedup probably reflects the narrower feature set.

name: Asmc
baseline: MASM (Microsoft Macro Assembler 6.15 and 10.0), also compared with JWasm and UASM
workload: Assemble time of a 21,000-line MASM-syntax source in a forum user's test.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: 1200 ms for Asmc versus 1800 ms for MASM 6.15 and 10.0 (1.5x, derived from snippet data), 1480 ms JWasm, 1630 ms UAsm64; a different poster in the same snippet puts Asmc 'about 25-30% faster than UAsm'. The README itself makes no speed claim.
tradeoffs: Written in assembly (MASM syntax, self-hosted); runs on Windows and Linux; GPL licence; MASM compatibility is not perfect (the project adds its own macro/language extensions and claims MASM v14 AVX-512 support while its Version macro is v10).
caveats: The MASM-compatible assembler timing numbers appear only in a WebSearch result snippet of a masm32.com forum thread (page unreachable here: ENOTFOUND), recorded as 'snippet only'; the same thread says on a 21,000-line source MASM 6.15 and 10.0 took 1800 ms each, UAsm64 1630 ms, JWasm 1480 ms and AsmC 1200 ms. Anecdotal forum measurement, no hardware, flags or versions seen. One poster in the same snippet says the same extensions make him distrust the tool, and another snippet claim of a '7-8x' speed-up over MASM contradicts the 1.5x timing above.

name: MaxAs
baseline: cuBLAS sgemm (NVIDIA's library kernels, compiled by NVIDIA's toolchain)
workload: Hand-scheduled single-precision GEMM kernels written in Maxwell SASS and assembled with MaxAs, versus cuBLAS sgemm, on large (4096) and small matrices.
claimed_speedup: SGEMM walkthrough: 'performing as much as 25% over cublas' for small matrices (64-thread version) and 'beating cublas by 4.8%' at size 4096 (256-thread version); about 98% of theoretical peak on GM107 and 96% on GM204. Absolute GFLOPS appear only in chart images.
hardware: NVIDIA GM204 (Maxwell) at a sustained 1607 MHz core clock and 8000 MHz memory; GM107 also mentioned. Card model and cuBLAS version are not stated on the page.
tradeoffs: Assembler for NVIDIA Maxwell SASS only (GTX 9xx era), written in Perl; the repository is archived and Intel has discontinued the project. Gains come from hand-written kernels and scheduling, not from the assembler alone.
caveats: First-party wiki claim; exact per-size GFLOPS are only in images, and the page names no cuBLAS version, CUDA version or flags. The speedup is of a hand-written kernel against a 2015-era library, not of the assembler against GNU as, NASM or MASM. Treat as a reference, not a general assembler win.
found_via: GitHub: README and SGEMM wiki page of NervanaSystems/maxas, found while looking for GPU (SASS) assemblers

name: SuperCoder
baseline: gcc -O3 compiled assembly (output quality)
workload: Runtime speedup of LLM-rewritten x86 assembly versus the gcc -O3 assembly on a benchmark of 8,072 real-world programs averaging 130 lines (CodeNet-derived), with test-based correctness checks.
claimed_speedup: Per WebSearch result text of arXiv 2505.11480 only (paper not opened): the RL-fine-tuned Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct model reaches a 95.0% test pass rate and a 1.46x average speedup over gcc -O3; the strongest baseline LLM (Claude-opus-4) reaches 51.5% pass rate and 1.43x average speedup.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 baseline stated in search-result text; flags and timing harness (hyperfine) not stated in the README

caveats: Numbers come from search-result text only; the repo README has no results section and states no hardware or compiler flags. Averages are over test-passing programs as reported by the authors, so failed rewrites are excluded from the speedup mean (not verified on the paper). Preprint status; 2 commits in the repo.

name: Fadec
baseline: libopcodes, Capstone and Zydis (x86 decoding libraries)
workload: Decoding x86-32 and x86-64 instructions with a lookup-table decoder; a separate x86-64 encoder is included.
claimed_speedup: 'Fadec is significantly faster than libopcodes, Capstone, or Zydis due to the absence of high-level abstractions and the small lookup table' (no numbers); encoder API v2 'about 3x faster than v1' (internal comparison).

name: SLOTHY
baseline: unscheduled 'clean' hand-written assembly and prior hand-optimized implementations of the same kernels (ML-KEM and ML-DSA NTTs, FFT, X25519); no compiler baseline stated on the pages opened
workload: Instruction scheduling, register allocation and software pipelining of hand-written Arm AArch64, Armv8.1-M and RISC-V assembly for cryptographic and DSP kernels.
claimed_speedup: README: SLOTHY has been used 'to provide the fastest known implementations of various cryptographic and DSP primitives' (ML-KEM and ML-DSA NTTs for Cortex-A55/A72/M55/M85, FFT for Cortex-M55/M85, X25519 for Cortex-A55); no speedup numbers on any page opened. Related adoption number: the AWS-LC pull request that imported the s2n-bignum X25519 rewrite (partly SLOTHY-generated) reports 12867.1 to 22361.9 ops/sec ('74% speedup') on Graviton 2, but that gain is not attributable to SLOTHY alone.
hardware: Targets Cortex-M55, M85, A55 (supported), A72, Cortex-X/Neoverse-V, Apple M1 (experimental) and XuanTie C908
stars_or_usage: 352 stars; adopted in AWS-LC / s2n-bignum, Arm EndpointAI CMSIS DSP and mlkem-native
tradeoffs: Microarchitecture-specific by design: each output is scheduled for one core model (portability note: code tuned for Cortex-A55 is not tuned for other cores). Solver time is seconds to minutes for under 50 instructions and minutes to hours for up to 150 instructions; larger kernels need heuristics. Python tool using Google OR-Tools.
caveats: The paper (CHES 2024, eprint 2022/1303) and its numbers could not be opened (eprint.iacr.org blocked), so no measured speedup is confirmed. The repo ships the clean and optimized sources and a reproduction artifact (paper/, paper/artifact) but cycle benchmarks need physical boards and were not run or read. The AWS-LC PR (#1469) was closed unmerged and mixes an algorithm change with SLOTHY scheduling.
found_via: github.com/topics/superoptimization (WebFetch); opened the slothy README, paper/README.md, LICENSE and AWS-LC / s2n-bignum PR pages

name: hash-wasm
baseline: Pure-JavaScript hash libraries in V8 (crypto-js, spark-md5, jsSHA, noble-hashes, node-forge, xxhashjs) and other WASM hash packages
workload: Hash throughput at 32-byte and 1 MB inputs (MD5, SHA1, SHA256, SHA3-512, XXHash64) plus PBKDF2-SHA512 and Argon2id ops/s, in Chrome via the hash-wasm-benchmark app
claimed_speedup: 1 MB throughput: MD5 850.31 MB/s vs spark-md5 171.73 and crypto-js 46.71 MB/s; SHA256 426.16 vs noble-hashes 110.02, crypto-js 65.17 MB/s; SHA3-512 234.40 vs noble-hashes 14.19 MB/s; XXHash64 15 989 MB/s vs xxhashjs 42.26 MB/s; PBKDF2-SHA512 588 ops vs crypto-js 29 ops; Argon2id 438 ops vs argon2-browser 213 ops
compiler_and_flags: clang --target=wasm32 -flto -O3 -nostdlib -fno-builtin -ffreestanding (scripts/Makefile-clang, built in an Alpine 3.20.3 Docker image, compiler version not pinned); no WASM SIMD flags enabled (commented out in the Makefile)
tradeoffs: Each algorithm ships as a separate base64-embedded WASM binary, so there is a WASM instantiation cost on first use. Async init for the streaming createXXXX() API. Browsers and Node.js only.
caveats: The README table lists numbers for the README-stated library versions (hash-wasm 4.10.0) while the latest commit is 4.12.0. Numbers are first-party, produced by the author's own benchmark app (separate repo Daninet/hash-wasm-benchmark, source in src/ opened; the live app lives on github.io which was not reachable). Compiler version is not pinned. Node's native crypto module (OpenSSL) is not in the comparison, so this does not show it beats native hashing. XXHash64 1 MB figure (15 989 MB/s) is about equal to xxhash-wasm 1.0.2 (15 929 MB/s).

compiler_and_flags: asc (AssemblyScript 0.28.x) with -O3 --noAssert --uncheckedBehavior always --runtime incremental --enable bulk-memory (plus --enable simd for SIMD mode), then wasm-opt; run in V8 (d8, v8 15.1.42 per chart footer) with TurboFan (--no-liftoff). Source: scripts/run-bench.as.sh.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D (8 cores, 96 MB 3D V-Cache), 32 GB RAM, Linux 6.17 (README)
name: json-as
baseline: JavaScript built-in JSON.parse / JSON.stringify in V8 (also fast-json-parse and assemblyscript-json)
workload: End-to-end JSON deserialize (including allocating the destination object) and serialize throughput in MB/s on small payloads (19 B to 5.5 kB) and nine standard payloads from the yyjson and nativejson-benchmark corpora, with json-as compiled to Wasm by the AssemblyScript compiler (asc) and run in V8.
claimed_speedup: Deserialize, SWAR mode vs built-in JSON in V8: 1,321 vs 568 MB/s (1.1 kB payload), 5,734 vs 1,295 MB/s (5.5 kB payload), 2,196 vs 168 MB/s (108 B payload), 1,056 vs 401 MB/s (52 B alphabet string). Serialize, SIMD mode vs built-in JSON: 7,775 vs 1,062 MB/s (5.5 kB payload), 3,818 vs 696 MB/s (1.1 kB payload). Library comparison on a 5 KiB GitHub-repo payload (deserialize): json-as struct 5,636 MB/s, native JSON 547 MB/s, fast-json-parse 547 MB/s, assemblyscript-json 32 MB/s. Smallest-gain row: 3D Vector (19 B) deserialize, 356-444 vs 83 MB/s across the three typed modes, while the dynamic JSON.Obj path ties built-in JSON on that row (82 vs 83 MB/s). Numbers read from the chart images overview-deserialize.png, overview-serialize.png and library-deserialize.png on the docs branch (v1.5.0).
tradeoffs: Typed, schema-driven (struct) API: the build-time transform generates a specialised serializer per @json class, so it only competes with JSON.parse when the schema is known up front; dynamic JSON.Obj path is slower. Needs AssemblyScript toolchain and a Wasm host; builds use --noAssert and --uncheckedBehavior always, which removes bounds and assert checks. SIMD mode needs Wasm SIMD support.
caveats: Chart values are only in PNG/SVG images (read from the PNG), not in a text table. The JS baseline parses to generic JavaScript objects while json-as parses into typed structs, so work done differs. Per-row wins vary: JSON.Obj (dynamic) path is not always faster (Alphabet and UUIDv4 rows show 0, 3D Vector 82 vs 83 MB/s). Benchmark author is the library author. Chart footer shows a date of Jul 17 2026 and commit 0bb47d4; later commits exist on main.

name: Speedy.js
baseline: Plain JavaScript in V8 (Chrome 58) and SpiderMonkey (Firefox 53); Emscripten-compiled C++ shown alongside
workload: 14 small benchmark kernels (arrayReverse, doubleAdd, doubleCompare, fib, intCompare, isPrime, mergeSort, mergeSortInt, nsieve, simjs, tspArrayDouble, tspArrayInt, tspDouble, tspInt) compiled from a JavaScript subset to WebAssembly and compared with the same code run as JS.
claimed_speedup: Chart in the README (read from doc/benchmark.png): speedup vs JS, 100% means equal. The VMIL 2017 workshop abstract (seen in a search snippet only) says compute-intense code becomes up to four times faster and run-time fluctuation is halved. Chrome 58: fib 352%, isPrime 311%, nsieve 273%, mergeSortInt 140%, tspInt 134%, mergeSort 124%, arrayReverse 91%, doubleAdd 100%. Firefox 53: arrayReverse 444%, nsieve 399%, fib 288%, mergeSortInt 167%, mergeSort 157%, tspInt 138%, simjs 133%, intCompare 94%, doubleCompare 96%. Several kernels are 100% or below.
tradeoffs: Experimental compiler for a restricted JavaScript subset with an int type (custom TypeScript fork), needs a self-built LLVM with the WebAssembly target, calls from JS are async. Archived and tied to 2017 browsers.
caveats: Numbers are read from the README chart image doc/benchmark.png (Chrome 58.0.3029.110 and Firefox 53.0, 2017 engines); no hardware or flags stated. Peer-reviewed basis: Reiser and Blaeser, 'Accelerate JavaScript Applications by Cross-Compiling to WebAssembly', VMIL 2017 (ACM SIGPLAN workshop at SPLASH 2017); the paper and thesis pages could not be opened here (splashcon.org, ACM, OST blocked), only the abstract via a search snippet, so tier B rests on that abstract and a verifier with paper access should confirm. Mixed result: about half the kernels are at or near parity, and 2017 browsers are far from current engines.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch 'Accelerate JavaScript Applications by Cross-Compiling to WebAssembly Reiser Blaeser VMIL 2017' (SPLASH 2017 / VMIL 2017 program snippet), repo then opened on github.com

name: Cheerp
baseline: Emscripten (C/C++ to WebAssembly)
workload: Vendor release-note comparison of compiled benchmark execution speed on one benchmark machine, averaged over three runs (snippet only; the post could not be opened)
claimed_speedup: Cheerp 2.6rc1 release notes (search snippet): Cheerp output runs roughly 5% faster than Emscripten; Cheerp 3.0 post (snippet): about 7% smaller output and execution speed comparable to Emscripten
tradeoffs: Compiles C++ to WebAssembly and JavaScript; the vendor 3.0 post says multithreading and WebAssembly atomics were not yet supported at 3.0. Different JS/DOM interop model than Emscripten (can call DOM directly).
caveats: Snippet only: leaningtech.com blog pages were EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the speed claim comes from WebSearch snippets of vendor posts. The newest vendor wording is parity with Emscripten, not faster; the only independent comparison found (Palant, 2016, asm.js era) had Emscripten slightly ahead. Neither the cheerp-compiler nor the cheerp-meta README contains a benchmark. Treat as weak: faster-in-size and about equal in speed.

name: markdown-wasm
baseline: markdown-it, marked, commonmark.js and showdown (JavaScript) in Node.js / V8

name: md4w
language: Zig and C (md4c) compiled to WebAssembly
baseline: markdown-it (JavaScript) in Deno / V8; markdown-wasm (C compiled to wasm) also compared
workload: Parse and render the CommonMark spec markdown document (test/commonmark-spec.md) to HTML per iteration with deno bench.
claimed_speedup: README: about 2.5x faster than markdown-it. Screenshot in test/benchmark-screenshot.png: md4w 1.89 ms/iter (529.1 iter/s), markdown-wasm 2.16 ms/iter (462.0 iter/s), markdown-it 5.19 ms/iter (192.6 iter/s); 5.19/1.89 is 2.7x (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Needs async wasm init; the fast wasm is 270 KB gzipped versus 28 KB for the small build, which is slower; GFM support is partial (task lists, tables); markdown-it has a far larger plugin ecosystem.
caveats: Results are a terminal screenshot (no text table), single input file, single machine, one run. The harness is public (test/benchmark.js) so it can be rerun, but the Zig version is not stated, so the tier is held at C. The baseline pulls markdown-it 14.0.0 from esm.sh. Author's own benchmark.

compiler_and_flags: Scala.js linker with withUseWebAssembly(true), ESModule output, ES2022; engine versions Node.js 25, Chrome 137, Firefox 134, Safari 26 listed as supported
name: Scala.js WebAssembly backend
baseline: Scala.js JavaScript backend output run in V8 / Node.js (JS emitted code)
workload: Run-time of Scala.js programs compiled with the WasmGC backend versus the same programs compiled with the Scala.js JS backend, across the project's own benchmark set.
claimed_speedup: Scala.js website: for applications dominated by computation inside Scala code the Wasm output should be significantly faster than the JS output (geomean 30% lower run time across our benchmarks). Interop-heavy code may be significantly slower; generated code size about twice as large in fullLink mode.
tradeoffs: No @JSExport support, no multi-module emit, JSPI needed for js.async/js.await, JS interop calls slower, Wasm code about 2x larger than JS output.
caveats: The 30% geomean figure is a first-party sentence in the documentation with no benchmark list, machine, engine or harness named on that page; third-party recaps (VirtusLab blog, ICFP/SPLASH 2025 Wasm workshop abstract: up to 3.4x faster and 3.5x slower than JS and JVM targets) could not be opened. Baseline is Scala.js's own JS backend, not hand-written TypeScript.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: WebSearch 'Scala.js WebAssembly backend WasmGC performance benchmarks compared to JavaScript output' (ICFP/SPLASH 2025 workshop paper listing)

baseline: TensorFlow.js plain JavaScript CPU backend in V8 (Chrome); also compared with the WebGL backend
workload: MobileNet V2 and Face Detector model inference time in ms (average of 200 runs) on iPhone X, Pixel 4, desktop Windows and Linux machines, Chrome 79
claimed_speedup: MobileNet V2: WASM backend about 3X-11.5X faster than the plain JS backend (ThinkPad X1 Gen6 Linux 122.7 ms WASM vs 1489.4 ms plain JS; WASM + SIMD 34.6 ms; WASM + SIMD + threads 12.4 ms); Face Detector: about 8.2X-19.8X faster (Desktop Linux 12.6 ms vs 249.5 ms plain JS)

hardware: iPhone X, Pixel 4, desktop Windows, ThinkPad X1 Gen6 Linux, desktop Linux; CPU models not stated; Chrome 79.0

name: xxhash-wasm
baseline: xxhashjs (pure JavaScript, 64-bit emulated via cuint) in Node/V8; also Node built-in crypto md5 and sha1
workload: Benchmark.js ops/sec hashing random strings from 1 byte to 100,000,000 bytes (32-bit and 64-bit xxHash)
claimed_speedup: xxhash-wasm 32-bit up to 90 times faster and 64-bit up to 350 times faster than xxhashjs; at 1 byte 4,438,501 ops/sec (64-bit) vs xxhashjs 11,896 ops/sec (64-bit); vs Node crypto md5 342,924 ops/sec at 1 byte; at 100,000,000 bytes 34.56 ops/sec vs xxhashjs 0.13 ops/sec (64-bit)
compiler_and_flags: wasm-opt --enable-bulk-memory -O4 src/xxhash.wat -o src/xxhash.wasm (package.json build-wasm script); benchmarks in the repo bench/ folder via Benchmark.js
hardware: x64 MacBook Pro (exact CPU model not stated), Node 17.3 for the Node-crypto table; hardware and Node version of the xxhashjs table not stated
tradeoffs: Needs async WebAssembly instance creation (about 2 ms in Node, about 1 ms in the browser) before first use. 64-bit API uses BigInt, which adds overhead for small inputs. Non-cryptographic hash only.
caveats: The headline ratio is against xxhashjs, a slow pure-JS port that emulates 64-bit math with cuint, not against a tuned JS hash. The Node crypto comparison is md5 and sha1, not another non-cryptographic hash. No official native xxHash C baseline in the table. Hardware only partly stated.
